prompt: What does the lesson say to write down before designing any layout?

choices.text: A list of every chart the data allows
choices.why: That starts from the data, not the reader.

choices.text: The colour palette the company uses
choices.why: Colours come much later.

choices.text: The tool the dashboard will be built in
choices.why: The tool does not decide what the reader needs.

choices.text: The questions the dashboard answers, and for whom
choices.why: Right, with who reads it and what they do with the answer.

prompt: A manager hands over fifteen questions for one dashboard. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Use smaller charts so that all fifteen fit
choices.why: Fitting them is not the same as answering them.

choices.text: Put fifteen tabs along the top of the screen
choices.why: That hides the questions behind clicks.

choices.text: Answer the five easiest and drop the rest
choices.why: Ease is not importance.

choices.text: Split it into several dashboards of a few questions each
choices.why: Right. Three to five questions per screen.

prompt: A number on the dashboard would not change anybody's decision, whatever its value. What should happen to it?

choices.text: Move it to the top left so it is seen
choices.why: That is the place for the most important number.

choices.text: Show it larger so that it gets noticed
choices.why: Size would claim an importance it lacks.

choices.text: Colour it red to mark it as optional
choices.why: Red would make it louder, not quieter.

choices.text: Leave it off the screen, since nobody acts on it
choices.why: Right. Each extra tile takes attention from the others.

prompt: Where does the most important number go on a dashboard read left to right?

choices.text: In the bottom right corner, as a conclusion
choices.why: That is where unread things end up.

choices.text: In the exact centre of the screen
choices.why: The eye starts at the top left, not the centre.

choices.text: In a tooltip that appears on hover
choices.why: Hidden numbers are not read at a glance.

choices.text: At the top left, where reading starts
choices.why: Right, where the eye starts.

prompt: Two charts on a dashboard are drawn the same size. What does that tell the reader?

choices.text: That they share the same data source
choices.why: Size says nothing about sources.

choices.text: That the two of them matter equally to the reader
choices.why: Right, whether or not anybody meant it.

choices.text: That they should be read at the same time
choices.why: The eye reads one thing at a time.

choices.text: Nothing at all; size is a technical choice
choices.why: Size is read as importance.

prompt: Put the parts of the lesson's dashboard layout in order, from the top of the screen down.
Eye-tracking studies found an F-shaped scanning pattern. On what kind of page?

choices.text: Pages that are dense with rows of text
choices.why: Right. Sparse pages show more of a Z.

choices.text: Pages built around one single large photograph
choices.why: The F comes from rows of text.

choices.text: Pages written right to left
choices.why: There the pattern would mirror.

choices.text: Pages viewed on a phone held sideways
choices.why: The study was about the content, not the device.

prompt: Match each Gestalt principle to what it says.

pairs.right: things in one box form a group
things that look alike are the same kind

prompt: How should the gaps on a dashboard be set?

choices.text: Smaller inside groups, larger between them
choices.why: Right. Equal gaps say there are no groups.

choices.text: Equal everywhere, for a tidy grid
choices.why: Tidy, and it hides the grouping.

choices.text: As small as possible, to fit more charts
choices.why: Then nothing groups at all.

choices.text: Larger around the charts the designer likes
choices.why: Gaps should follow the subjects, not taste.

prompt: Things placed close together are read as a group. Gestalt calls this the principle of ___.
Two bar charts side by side are meant to be compared. What should they share?

choices.text: A legend placed between them
choices.why: Direct labels are better, and a legend does not fix scales.

choices.text: Exactly the same number of bars each
choices.why: The scale matters, not the count.

choices.text: The same value scale on both of them
choices.why: Right, or the comparison they invite cannot be made.

choices.text: A different colour each, to tell them apart
choices.why: Same subject, same colour.

prompt: A card shows "180,682" and its label. What does it still need before it can be judged?

choices.text: A larger font
choices.why: Size does not say whether it is good.

choices.text: A pie chart beside it
choices.why: A pie of one number shows nothing.

choices.text: A coloured background
choices.why: Colour without a comparison means nothing.

choices.text: A comparison
choices.why: Right: against last year, a target, or the same month.

prompt: What is a sparkline?

choices.text: A word-sized line chart without axes
choices.why: Right. It shows the path to the number.

choices.text: A flashing number that draws attention
choices.why: That would be decoration, and an annoying one.

choices.text: The gridline under a card's number
choices.why: Cards do not need gridlines.

choices.text: A coloured bar under the title
choices.why: That carries no data.

prompt: December 2025 had 20,586 orders and December 2024 had 16,663. What is the growth in percent, to one decimal place?
Median delivery time rose by two minutes, and the card shows the rise in green. What is wrong?

choices.text: Times should be shown in hours, not minutes
choices.why: Minutes suit delivery times.

choices.text: A change of two minutes is too small to show
choices.why: Whether it matters is the reader's call; the colour is the problem.

choices.text: Up is bad here, so green says the opposite
choices.why: Right. Colour the change only when its meaning is right.

choices.text: Cards should never show a change
choices.why: A comparison is what makes a card readable.

prompt: A card is labelled just "orders". What is missing from the label?

choices.text: The colour
choices.why: A label is words.

choices.text: The period
choices.why: Right: "orders in 2025".

choices.text: The company's name
choices.why: The dashboard already says whose it is.

choices.text: The font size
choices.why: That is styling, not content.

prompt: What does the five-second test check first?

choices.text: Whether the page loads quickly enough
choices.why: Speed matters, but the test is about reading.

choices.text: Whether the colours match the brand
choices.why: Brand colours are not the question.

choices.text: Whether every number is correct
choices.why: Five seconds cannot check that.

choices.text: Whether the hierarchy works
choices.why: Right: did they name the number you meant?

prompt: After five seconds, a colleague says "there was a pie chart". What does that tell you?

choices.text: The pie was the loudest thing there
choices.why: Right, louder than the number you meant.

choices.text: The colleague likes pie charts
choices.why: The test measures the screen, not the person.

choices.text: The dashboard needs one more pie
choices.why: That would make it worse.

choices.text: Five seconds was too short a test
choices.why: Five seconds is the point.

prompt: Find each part of this dashboard.
hint: The comparison is the small triangle under the first number.

prompt: Which of these belong on the lesson's checklist? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Every tile is the same size
choices.why: Equal sizes hide the hierarchy.

choices.text: Each chart has a colour of its own
choices.why: Colours should mean the same thing everywhere.

choices.text: Every number has its period and unit
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Charts that will be compared share a scale
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The main chart is the biggest thing
choices.why: Right.

prompt: According to the lesson, how do dashboards usually get worse?

choices.text: One reasonable request at a time
choices.why: Right, which is why the test is worth repeating.

choices.text: Through a deliberate redesign gone wrong
choices.why: Rarely by design.

choices.text: When the data source changes its format
choices.why: That breaks them; it does not crowd them.

choices.text: When the tool is upgraded to a new version
choices.why: Tools are not the usual cause.
